posts.title: Ask HN: Where do you see Software in 5 years?
posts.text: I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm anxious about the future and lack the foresight to form any opinion on what to do next. For context, I'm a L4 SWE that has more or less say 5-10 yrs of exp. I've enjoyed my work throughout my career, AI makes me ship more, much more than I could do 3 years ago. I feel I use it well and it translates into really good software. That said, what do you think happens in years to come with the Software industry in general? Do you think we'll go through a massive erosion of jobs? What's your perspective on that? I'm asking because I honestly don't know what to do: I can try to always keep up to date with newest technologies, best practices, but I'm only me; if the demand for SWEs and jobs falls to the floor, I'm not sure I'll always get a place at the table (i.e. land a job) and I'm wondering whether I should try to do something else in some other industry. It feels weird to be in a good position in life and still constantly worry about it getting worse.

comments.text: Everyone wants a crystal ball on where this will end up. Reality is none of us have any idea - there's a risk to any decision you make. I can make a decent sounding argument for any side, simply because there's no way to base it on any evidence at this point. The onramp for coding becoming easier means non-tech people finally have a cheaper way to try out business ideas for domains they're experts in. Many of those will succeed and will need to hire developers, massively increasing the demand. Coding becoming easier means many more people will jump in, reducing wages rapidly. While there might be some work available, it'll mostly be low paid. Now that one person can do the job of 5, 4/5 will be laid off and we'll all struggle to get work. Now that one person can do the job of 5, AND there will be an increased demand for more developers from more businesses popping up, we'll be paid a hell of a lot more for the value we can generate. The speed of code generation is going to catch up to us in the form of tech debt, and we'll see the outcome of that in 12 months as codebase development slows to a halt and AI can't deal with it. We'll be swamped with work. AI will continue to develop at a rapid pace and take over all white-collar work and the world will change as we know it. Take your pick. I don't know.
comments.author: tripleee

comments.text: My guess is as good as (or probably worse!) than the next person's, but I see one of two things happening: A return to personal computing as it existed in the early 80s, where owning a computer meant writing your own software for it, with exceptions. Alternatively, hardware scarcity meaning everything is forced to the cloud.

Existing tools, systems, frameworks and such just won't matter, would just slow down AI. Replacing complete vertical system silos will be done in a single, crazy step, efficient to run, secured by an awesome security AI. I recently retired after working in software development from 1975 to 2025 encompassing punch cards to AI.
comments.author: jimcollinswort1

comments.text: In 5 years time software will exist in 3 silos. It's really not any different today, except the talent will continue to diverge. Silo 1 - This will be employers strongly forcing AI for most task completion. This will be most large corporate employers and most start ups. There will be little to no working knowledge of the internals of large applications and these employers will bleed money on outside consultants to occasionally provide manual maintenance and security hot fixes. Everything will continue to look good from the outside, but really its a messy house of cards. Silo 2 - This will be institutional shops of skilled experts. Game companies that own internally developed rendering engines, kernel developers, independent open source, and systems architects come to mind. These will be people that might occasionally dabble in AI for various things, but they manually modify their code. These are experts who do not gain productivity by offloading their greatest challenges to AI. Silo 3 - The consulting class. This is where the money will be. Technology design firms already do most of this, but the problems these consultants solve for their clients will be greater and the clients will be less capable. These people will explode in demand, but supply will likely remain unchanged, because experts are hard to grow and the corporate world won't produce them. --- I also predict the job recruitment industry will struggle as demand for talent stratifies, because software as an industry struggles to identify talent. This problem will remain unsolved until something catastrophic happens and most employers need to simultaneously unload liability in ways they are currently forced to accept it internally. Fear of bankruptcy, loss of money, and complete destruction of business are not strong enough motivators to move the needle on this.

posts.title: GitLab 19.6.0 is out and still vulnerable to Ruby2Shell and NGINX2Root
posts.text: What's going on at GitLab? They released their usual monthly release 19.6.0 to their package repos (https://packages.gitlab.com/gitlab/gitlab-ee/ubuntu/jammy/pool/main/g/gitlab-ee/) but did not announce it at all as of 3.5h after release (https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/all-releases.xml, https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/19/gitlab-19-6-released/). But more annoyingly, this release does not address ruby2shell or nginx2root, nor do patches for their older releases exist yet and there's no communication on any of this (that I can find). root@gitlab:~# cat /opt/gitlab/embedded/service/gitlab-rails/VERSION 19.6.0-ee root@gitlab:~# /opt/gitlab/embedded/sbin/nginx -version nginx version: nginx/1.31.7 root@gitlab:~# /opt/gitlab/embedded/bin/ruby --version ruby 3.3.13 (2026-10-23 revision af48f08f21) [x86_64-linux] root@gitlab:~# lsb_release -a No LSB modules are available. Distributor ID: Ubuntu Description: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS Release: 22.04 Codename: jammy Multiple MRs were created in their repos 14-15 hours ago, no urgency visible. Heres 2 I found: https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/omnibus-gitlab/-/merge_requests/10138 https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/omnibus-gitlab/-/merge_requests/10139

comments.text: The pre-release info on 19.6.0 says that it addresses nginx2shell: https://docs.gitlab.com/update/versions/gitlab_19_changes/#n... There is also a workaround to disable http2 from NGINX and make that part safe. I'm leaving HTTP2 disabled for the forseeable future. - edit /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb - add lines: gitlab_rails['nginx']['http2_enabled'] = false nginx['http2_enabled'] = false - save and run: gitlab-ctl reconfigure - finally run: gitlab-ctl restart nginx There is no workaorund for Ruby2Shell though :( As it was just dropped last night, well after they would have started testing etc for 19.6.0, it's no surprise it's not in there. Also, since they konw 19.6.0 has Ruby2Shell in it, it's not much surprise they haven't been promoting it, or that they are scrambling. GitLab is such a huge beast that it can't be quick to get changes made and run through tests for everything. Who knows what else the runtime update caused to fail. I imagine they are working on it.. meanwhile I firewalled the web of any of the ones I take care of. IMO having gitlab open to the public web is insanity personified.. I sure wouldn't do that with my instance!

posts.title: Ask HN: If AI tools are so good, why isn't your bug backlog empty?
posts.text: A lot of people outside tech ask me if AI is going to replace programmers and I just think: if that were the case we should be running out of things to do The bug backlog should be empty and we've caught up to every feature request from PMs to the point that we are bottlenecked on the business side But that does not seem to be the case with my own company or most devs I talk to in the industry So what gives?

comments.text: I don't know if I'm doing something wrong but bug fixing with AI has always been a crapshoot. You can absolutely tell an agent to fix an issue, and it will fix that issue, but the vast majority of the time that solution will be by adding code to cover the specific symptom in the bug report. It rarely considers or recommends solutions that have tradeoffs that may change behavior but will eliminate an entire class of similar bugs. This is mostly a problem of agents not having the autonomy of managing an entire project and having the ability to make tradeoffs to increase simplicity or maintainability, but when given that autonomy no AI model I've used uses that privilege to write simpler, more maintainable code.
comments.author: frostiness

comments.text: All my solo project backlogs _are_ empty. For my team projects, I still need my teammates to review code, so that bottlenecks how quickly we can burn down the backlog. If I didn't need code review I would have the backlog burned down in weeks, but I'd create a bunch of outages in the process (we do catch things in code review!) Also, some of my solo projects are gamedev-related, and gamedev is also bottlenecked on actually playing your game to see if its fun :) but it is great to get out of a 2 hour playtest session with notes and have a new build in like 15 minutes with the feedback incorporated.
comments.author: td521534f12

comments.text: It pretty much is? Every easily-described bug has been fixed. The only things that remain are "this isn't wrong per se, it just violates customer expectations" and someone needs to figure out what the product should do in this case. We burnt through our backlog of "obviously we should do this when we have time" stuff in the spring. It was pretty fun to kill pretty much all of my multi-year refactor and cleanup list. Now we are pretty much bottlenecked on the business side.
comments.author: fishtoaster

comments.text: Because AI is better at finding bugs than at fixing them. It is not good at writing bug-free code either. AI and humans don't make the same bugs. So AI may find bugs that are easily overlooked by humans while at the same time being incredibly stupid on some other parts.
comments.author: GuB-42

comments.text: > The bug backlog should be empty I don't follow. Maybe it's just me, but I've never worked at a company and on any substantial product that had an empty bug backlog. If a bug queue is empty, the product is either not used much (or not a priority), not tested well enough, or not monitored enough. I don't know that a world where AI has mostly replaced programmers is a world with an empty bug queue. While AI is reducing the _quantity_ of programmers needed in many cases, it is also an output multiplier for the remaining programmers, while often raising the bug-to-code ratio. AI has led to more output, more projects, and more bugs.
comments.author: yokuze

comments.text: If your team and product had a large backlog before thats not going to change. AI tools amplify whatever it is you do so if you've been ignoring bugs and focusing most of the time on new features, AI isn't going to magically change what a team is working on. On a technical level, take your average NullPointerException or the equivalent in whatever language you use. Ask AI to go fix it and it will sanely wrap or check for nulls in that piece of code. Ask a lead or senior engineer to fix it and they will (hopefully) start with "why is this data null? it shouldn't be" and then trace back through logs or data, try to recreate with a real scenario and not only fix that bug but find there's an unhandled scenario somewhere else in the code base. Someone could prompt the AI to expand further and do a root cause analysis but do you trust it to find things and fix them properly?
comments.author: mattbrewsbytes

comments.text: AI only can improve velocity if it mostly works unsupervised. But most people don't trust their agents to run alone. And to build that trust will take some time, people will need to learn how to use AI effectively. I think the PS3 hardware could be a good analogy. It was really powerful, but nobody really knew how to use it. After a few years people got really good at it . And you can view this evolution by the improvement of graphical fidelity we got over the years.

comments.text: Parkinson's Law: "Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson%27s_Law
comments.author: fritzo

comments.text: I'm in devops, not programming, so slightly different. I can say our backlog of absolutely essential jobs that we haven't been able to get around to for the last 5 years is absolutely being smashed out one by one. A lot of this is unattended server migrations running over night being validated the next day. The backlog as a whole though is growing as we have AI continually probing the infrastructure and various code bases looking for new security concerns or ways to improve performance and save money. Directly as a result of this, our cloud costs dropped massively in the last 6 months with only very minimal impact on performance. I absolutely see a time in the not too distant future where all our infrastructure tech debt has been cleaned up, the security situation is as good as we can get it, the backlog has completely emptied and some of my team will be surplus to requirements.

I finally got him to give Claude Code a go like three weeks ago and it's changed everything for them. He's expecting to clear his bug backlog by the end of the year. It's been incredible for them. He's improved stability, improved performance, and reduced memory footprint of his Windows Forms application. For him, it really is helping him crush his backlog. comments.author: jjice

comments.text: I think building new code up to a functional, code and security standard will get easier and easier with AI and we may reach a point where the list of bugs is shorter. However, based on what I have seen building my software factory (7 agents, each with their own roles) and iterating on it, an agent will only have a certain amount of context and scrutiny it can dedicate. So I found that segregation of resonsibilities between agents (which one does which checks) + automated checks and tests are really important. However, I don't know yet to what extent. It feels like my factory is getting better and better, but there are still things being sent back, and still there is an occasional helper that is getting re-written a bit differently (even if I have a tech lead agent who is looking at the whole code). So I can only imagine the complexity for a legacy app or a huge app where even multiple agents cannot have enough context to write code that considers code and functions next to the feature it is working on. I don't think that agents at this time can have the capability of a senior dev who really knows the system. The best thing we can do is to distill how a senior dev looks at the system from all different angles and write instructions as clear and short as possible. Then iterate and test continuously with measuring the outcomes. At least that's what I'm trying to do.
comments.author: cmadar

comments.text: Last year during the summer I had a bunch of things I wanted to do to improve on the trading system I was working on. A bunch of things that were mostly fiddly, which I had estimated would take me 6 months. Someone told me to try out Claude Code during my holiday. I learned the backstory of Sauron with a friend while getting the entire backlog cleaned up. Things worked, better and faster and more maintainable. Did I run out of things to do? Well, the firm I was with didn't know what they wanted built, so it was a lot of not getting anything done while waiting for them. But the things they had previously wanted, yes, they were done.

In my position, it wouldn't really matter how good AI is, because when we find a bug it will often take an hour long meeting, or even multiple meetings, just to figure out what a given behavior should actually be before we can even attempt to fix it.
comments.author: pickleglitch

comments.text: For my personal projects: 4 have zero backlog of any sort. 1 has a fleet of agents working through some product improvements that I postponed until the very end of the project. It's a very rote "rebuild this game on a modern engine" project to resurrect a game I developed 20 years ago, and there's a few small improvements I want to make to the game that deviate from the original. Today is day 5 of the rebuild, so it's not exactly a long-lived project per se -- but the bots did identify a bunch of defects in the original game and addressed them as part of the conversion project. 1 has: - A few flaky tests to clean up. - A couple heisenbugs that I can't pin down until I get a couple PCs for testing (3D graphics stuff is Fun<tm>). - A whole lot of features that consist of one sentence I wrote down to avoid losing track of an idea, and which I may or may not ultimately choose to implement at all. - A couple issues that can't proceed until a human gets involved. I.E. I need to go through the hassle of setting up a corporation and setting up accounts with the various gate keepers (Apple, Google, Valve). The biggest bottlenecks for me, at this moment are -- in descending order: 1. Running the linters / test suites / build processes for two of my projects completely slam my machine (load average hit 290 earlier today with 3 agents running things across the 2 game dev projects; CircleCI / Github Actions would be waaaay too expensive so I'm running it all locally until I can set up a CI runner node). 2. My bandwidth for acceptance testing, and other human-only work (read: game balance / play experience) 3. Weekly usage caps for fixed-price plans from the three services I use. Setting aside my relatively unusual circumstances: At any business, you're going to have a problem of information rot when it comes to a backlog. The person who recorded a defect or feature request may not remember enough context to make it actionable (or they may not be at the org anymore). The assumptions underpinning the issue may or may not hold anymore (and it may not be clear which situation you're in). Etc. Plus, there's going to be a not-unreasonable risk aversion to making changes that are in peripheral areas of the system that don't get a lot of attention -- lest fixing one issue cause some unexpected but undesirable outcome. A lot of it mostly boils down to either "institutional knowledge gap" or "acceptance testing is a bottleneck".
comments.author: jfrisby

posts.title: Ask HN: When was the last time you thought "that's bad API design"?
posts.text: I used to be irrationally impressed when I saw good API design and docs. Now I can't remember the last time I sat down and spent meaningful time reading docs for a platform. I've just gotten in the habit of pointing Claude at them or using a service like Context7 for the past year or so. As a consumer, I've realized that I'm not even sure which services I use that have good or badly designed APIs. If you maintain an API, have you changed how you write docs now that the main reader is probably an LLM?

comments.text: Any API where a GET request quietly changes state gets me every time. Inconsistent error formats are a close second.

posts.title: Rant: Gemini 4 does not make any sense
posts.text: On November 18th, Google released another model, this one called Neon. Making it the fourth model in just 2 months. OpenAI makes sense: Luna-Terra-Sol-Astra. Moon is smaller than earth, earth is smaller than sun and I can forgive them for not knowing that sun is also a star. Anthropic is even better: Haiku-Sonnet-Opus-Mythos/Fable. Haiku is an extremely short poem, Sonnet is a bit longer, Opus is very long and Mythos is extremely long. Ok, Fable does not exactly really fit in there, but they came up with it after they only had the three models, so we had time to adjust. Also, Claude told me: Fable is basically Mythos with extra safety, and a fable is a story with a moral. Now, I want you to think back to those high school chemistry classes. Which is bigger neon or carbon or hydrogen or argon? Impossible right? The correct answer, hydrogen, carbon, neon, argon, doesn't even match with model capabilities. To make things worse, there is no consistency, they are combining noble gases with other non-metals. You can't even say they went for easy names, helium, is not in there as an example. They really should have gone with just noble gasses: helium, neon, argon and xenon (skipping krypton to not confuse with kryptonite) I'm glad that Google is sort of back in the race, but they should really invest in someone who is not AI-pilled to come up with these names. PS don't get me started on Meta, wtf is a glimmer?

comments.text: > wtf is a glimmer? Really? Muse, Glimmer, Spark, Wonder — all words regarding inspiration/discovery/creativity. Glimmer being a word for a hint of light or hope, or an inkling of an idea or potential discovery. As good a set of names as any.
comments.author: dofm

Hydrogen is light and versatile, so that makes sense...kind of. Along came the Helix leak. Never heard of that element before. And now we have Neon. Which has a hallucination rate between Hydrogen and Carbon...but is named after a noble gas. Yep. Agreed. Not sure what's going on anymore.

posts.title: Ask HN: When does your app need its own UI vs. using it via MCP?
posts.text: I'd love to hear HN user's views on when they think an app their building needs a UI vs just supplies data via MCP to Claude/ChatGPT. If Claude/ChatGPT is where the bulk of work is done in the future (perhaps analogous to a general purpose computer) then how should app developers build in this world?

comments.text: UI is must-have if your users want any sort of precision, determinism, or certainty. UI is faster than giving complete-enough instructions to an LLM for tasks below a certain complexity level — and that threshold rises with your user’s skill and familiarity with the task and how opinionated they are about how it should be done.
comments.author: apothegm

comments.text: I'm experimenting with this balance now -- I built and launched a small analytics service (basic web tracking) that uses the web UI for sign-up through Cloudflare Access and provides minimal instructions on connecting your agent to MCP. There's minimal reporting post-login about the sites you're tracking, but site setup, configuration, and reporting is all done through MCP with your agent. It's working for my minimal needs right now (traffic over time, plotting visits on a map) and is a good way to figure out how I want to do reporting rather than building a more general purpose reporting interface.
comments.author: reagent

comments.text: First of all, it comes down to product positioning. Most of the apps I build are for my own work or collaborative reasoning tasks. Sometimes I build not just apps, but also web services and assorted small tools. My philosophy is to minimize UI as much as possible and keep interfaces lean. Anything that can run in the background stays out of the user’s view — that’s the product perspective. But when I build an app to accelerate my own research work, I tend to go for more complex UI layouts, laying out the full research workflow visibly on the interface.

posts.title: Interesting Learnings Working for a Startup
posts.text: 1. product isn't important, sales is important 2. infra isn't important, talent to build it is important 3. which stack you use to build the product isn't important, business taste is important 4. pushing employees isn't the fastest way to ship, building a process from learnings is much more efficient share your learnings below

comments.text: Sales is easy when you have a good product. Ever tried selling a cup of coffee? Lasagna? An iPhone, even a used one? Selling a bad product is very difficult. Many founders jump from never having sold anything to trying to sell bad products. They pick up a lot of bad habits and none of the fundamentals; this includes things like being sleazy/pushy salespeople. Sales is simple: Find people who need the product and explain how it solves the problem. PMF is about the right sales channel for your product. Whether you want marketing, sales, branding, or customer success, it depends on your channel. For tech, you have PMF when $1 mil ARR looks like a goal, not a fantasy. Most of the time though, if you can't get a sale, it's a product problem. Many people don't realize that if it looks vibe coded, it's practically unfinished – it's not a proper product. You used to need about a third of development time dedicated to polish; these days it may be closer to two-thirds. Have you ever tried selling a latte? The latte art matters. It's not all functionality and features.

posts.title: Ask HN: Tips for transitioning from web development to embedded/firmware?
posts.text: I started my career 15+ years ago doing native development (c, c++, etc), but the last decade I've been doing fullstack web applications. I'd like to transition closer to my roots with a job doing primarily c, c++ or rust. The natural place seems to be in embedded development or firmware work. How feasible is the transition this late in the game? Any advice?

comments.text: I'd say just do it. You have been in the industry for 15+ years and you surely know how to network/do interviews. I feel that you are just hesitating or wait for some confirmations. I wrote similar posts so that's my guess, but please criticize me if I'm wrong. My point is, whoever has actually done the transition, their experience may not really help you a lot. They might have a cousin who actually refers them to the company; They might have worked 10 years of embedded projects as a hobby; They might be lucky because 5 years ago there were a huge opening somewhere. I heard of a metaphor about elevators -- Several people ride an elevator to floor 100, and a reporter asked them how they get there -- one of them said he did 1,000 push-ups, another said he read 2 books, and a third said he bumped his head against the elevator's walls. Those experience might be very well relevant, or not. But above all, copying others' experience, in THIS market, probably doesn't work. Now that you are 6 years senior than me regarding SWE experience, I think you already know what to do -- just do it.

comments.text: I've done both over my career (as well as some other stuff.) While they are very different, if you know C, it's not hard to transition. Doing some personal projects in the space may reawaken your C skills, and help demonstrate competence. Good luck!
comments.author: bruce511

comments.text: There are two issues: 1) transitioning your skills, and 2) persuading someone to hire/pay you for your new skills. Transitioning your skills is possible. But embedded is a different world and a different mindset. You a lot less RAM and a smaller CPU. You may have hard deadlines - the right answer can be wrong if it's too late. You may have multiple threads that have to share data and not corrupt it, no matter what order events occur in. In the worst case, you may not have logging available at all, and you may not have a debugger. (I think the worst I ever had to do was attach a logic analyzer to the address bus, triggered by a specific address, and then use it to look at past memory addresses in order to figure out what path of execution had got me to the point of the crash.) So, yeah. It's a different world. Learnable, but different. Getting someone to believe you can do it enough that they're willing to pay you: I don't have great advice there. I spent almost my whole career in embedded. It seems to me that it's easier to get from there into, say, desktop programming, than it is to go the other way. Your best bet might be to emphasize your native development background, and count on there being a shortage of embedded people.

posts.title: Claude Gets Hella Paranoid
posts.text: Mm, so I hesitate to write this, because my own AI agents might read it. But what the hell. I've got this crappy little $300 PC on my network hooked up to my projector, that I mostly use to serve Jellyfin. So tired of it going down every time there's a Windows update, but I've been too lazy to get around to installing Ubuntu. Last night, when it went down, I asked my Claude-claw via Whatsapp if it could just SSH into it and set up a dual boot partition. Claude got as far as partitioning the drive and then starting asking hard questions , like (paraphrasing) "wait a minute. This crosses a line. I have now been asked to remote into a machine with a password, write a separate boot partition, and restart it. From this chat, you haven't really verified that you are you. If you're really there, and not just texting me, give me some proof". So I remoted in and created a TextEdit RTF file on the claw's desktop: "Hey, it's me, I'm asking you to remote into the PC". Claude read it and responded that it was the kind of proof it was looking for, real RTF headers and datestamps and such. I had proven I had physical access to the claw machine, (although not to the PC, but it seemed reassured anyway). A little while later, before triggering the Ubuntu installer, it put me through it all over again. I told Claude I was very thankful it was guarding my network so well, and I would go over and write a file on the target PC manually too. I'm not gonna lie: It was very fucking cool that it was able to do this without me ever needing to flash a USB drive, and by the time it was done it had set up Ubuntu, Tailscale and Jellyfin, and resolved the network issues; when I started watching a movie, the sound didn't work, so I prompted it and suddenly the sound came on as it wired up the HDMI adapter. Almost creepy. But I was pretty stunned at how reticent it was to do something relatively simple on my own network, with access I gave it. I think there must be a serious push right now to lock it down from monkeying with anything remotely, especially a BIOS.

comments.text: I suspect this paranoia will mainly impede honest people tinkering in their own home labs. This seems like another case of giving up freedom for security which usually doesn't end well.

comments.text: > Claude read it and responded that it was the kind of proof it was looking for That feels insecure. If it allows access to the remote system in any way before asking for proof, there will surely ways to trick that check. Will it grant itself more access just because you know the content of any file? Or does it have to be a new file? Does it have to contain a specific message, or could you just prove you know that a non-standard file exists at all? Could you use the read-only access in one session to gather the data for proving yourself in another session? It would be interesting to see exactly what the minimal acceptable "proof" actually is.

comments.text: A suite of high-dopamine games which use smart exercise bikes as the control interface. When playing Zwift, Rouvy, etc, I find that I get too competitive and ruin longer workouts by trying to keep up with or sprint past people who are much faster than me over long distances. This is bad for building stamina and endurance, but I get bored, and it's hard to fight boredom and physical strain both at once. I do not get bored sitting in front of Balatro, Raccoin, Tetris - anything with bright colours and satisfying noises and combos. The first finished prototype game is very simple: you sort coloured marbles. Higher watt output from the bike means marbles are blown, by wind, upwards as they roll across the screen. Lower watt output means they fall. Steady watt output means they move horizontally. Marble goes into correct hole -> satisfying noise. It rewards steady watt output over time, with minor adjustments, which is what I'm trying to work on right now. I was pretty amazed by how engaging I found it (total iPad baby brain). The miles really fly by - I get tired before I get bored. I think that next I'll either do a tower defence game, or a less-dopamine-rewarding game in the style of Kerbal Space Program. Taking your actual weight and watt output, putting a bike with wings into a physics engine, and the gameplay loop being unlocking increasingly large airplane pieces, and designing - then flying - increasingly ridiculous airborne bicycles seems like a compelling idea, though less good for fitness. The control surface being so limited - essentially one measurement which can either go up or down - is a really fun constraint for creativity.

comments.text: I worked at a sports company forever ago, and ever since then, I've wanted to build my own NBA scores + stats site. After a few false starts over the years, I have a new concept called Center Court that I'm so excited about. It's primary purpose is for live boxscores because all of the major sports sites have terrible UI/UX experiences. I always defaulted to ESPN.com but it's so slow and awful. Center Court is basically a bridge between espn.com (or nba.com) and more advanced stat focused sites that don't offer a good live experience. The technical implementation behind it is quite novel in this space too. Instead of storing computed statistics in a database, I store raw play by play payloads immutability and everything else is derived from those and can be trivially rebuilt so the event log is a derived cache of the payloads. Every stat on every page is a pure fold over the event log at request time; no derived number is stored. This enables some powerful features like being able to re-derive a game's entire state at any point of the game (or even a time range). Example game to try out: https://centercourtlive.com/game/0022600197 The site is meant to be extremely fast. It's all server-side rendered with progressive JS enhancements. URLs are immutable and cached behind a CDN. https://centercourtlive.com/

posts.title: Why is China treated as threat-actor but not India?
posts.text: Why do people balk at someone saying that the actions of India/Indians are a negative vector for technology but you can unblinkingly say China/Chinese in the same breath and they will agree? Doublethink/it's 1984/people are gullible cretins are not acceptable answers.

comments.text: America thinks it is a martial power, a superpower. This is completely wrong. America has always been a mercantile power. There's ample proof of this everywhere, but just consider this: Its greatest contribution to WWII was lend-lease, and its army has always been most famous for its logistics. China, too, has always been a mercantile power. The problem is that China has in recent decades played the game better, with smarter industrial policy and less concentration of wealth and power in the financial and service industries. So it is growing into becoming the engine of the future; the other side of the coin is that the American mercantile empire is cannibalizing and turning in on itself. The two have become interlocked. India is neither a martial nor a mercantile power. To both China and the US, it's largely irrelevant; there's no foreseeable future where India can displace America's concentration of wealth or China's development trajectory.
comments.author: A_D_E_P_T

comments.text: There's tons of political nuance about this. China is poised to dominate the technology scenario in the not so far future, and there's not much the US can do but to keep the crosshair of public opinion on them. At the same time, American businesses are laying off en masse while seeking H1B and hiring overseas. It does not help that there are some pretty high profile south-Asian CEOs and CTOs, which ends up attracting even more scrutiny.

comments.text: I think the default is to treat everyone else as a thread-actor and then rank them. Then in propagation you only talk about those you want to target based on the current political climate.
comments.author: ferguess_k

comments.text: China has been threatening to conquer Taiwan, for years. They have been building up their military, for years, with the explicitly stated goal of being able to conquer Taiwan. I haven't heard of India doing anything like that. China has had their secret police bullying and threatening Chinese people abroad, trying to get them to support China's positions. I haven't heard of India doing anything like that. China has been using critical materials - rare earths - as a political weapon. I haven't heard of India doing anything like that (though perhaps from lack of opportunity). Notice the wording - "I haven't heard". I do not absolutely say that India is not doing such things. But if they are, it doesn't make the press out here. But for the above reasons, we don't trust China, or at least the Chinese government. And then, China's government seems to have control over Chinese companies when they want it, in a way that India doesn't. For that reason, we don't trust critical tech from Chinese companies, because we fear that it may abruptly become unavailable to us in a crisis.

posts.title: Codeberg seems to have vanished from DNS
posts.text: It seems that at 06:30 UTC today, Codeberg's registrar has placed them on clientHold, which has removed them from the .org zone entirely.

comments.text: Apparently more and more registrars are "randomly" requiring clients to send copies of their passports and face selfies and other nonsense. I've heard namecheap is doing this and I emailed them and their answer was: > [snip] "It is correct that we do not require every customer to proceed with identity and payment verification. Unfortunately, we cannot specify the criteria; this information is internal." So randomly when they feel like it. Me and a number of customers are moving away from them immediately. Centralization of DNS is becoming a problem. Privacy rights are being trampled. Nobody should be collecting such images unless in emergencies, and they need to be liable when they misuse it.
